GAMBLING LOSS DEDUCTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How much of your winnings actually stays taxable now?

Starting with 2026 tax returns, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act caps your gambling-loss deduction at 90% of your winnings — even if you lost just as much as you won. This tool applies that cap to your own numbers and shows the "phantom income" it can create.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Tax year and filing details

Only itemizers can claim any gambling-loss deduction at all — this predates OBBBA. A professional gambler groups wagering losses with directly related business expenses before comparing against the cap.

2. Your numbers

Use your actual, substantiated winnings and losses for the year — W-2G forms, wagering tickets, or a session log. This calculator does not verify either figure.

Fill in your winnings and losses, then click Calculate.

Your gambling-loss deduction

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This computes one deduction cap — not your total itemized deductions, whether itemizing beats the standard deduction, other credits, or state tax treatment (many states do not allow the federal gambling-loss deduction at all).
  • Does not verify your figures. You supply winnings and losses directly; this tool does not check them against a W-2G, a session log, or any other record.
  • No state-by-state modeling. Several states disallow gambling-loss deductions entirely at the state level, independent of this federal cap.
  • Repeal is not modeled. Bills to restore the full 100% offset have been introduced but had not passed as of this tool's last fact-check — this calculator applies current law only.

Common questions

What is the new 90% gambling loss deduction limit?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, amended IRC Section 165(d) so that, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, your gambling-loss deduction is capped at the lesser of your actual, substantiated losses or 90% of your winnings. This is on top of the pre-existing rule that losses can never be deducted beyond winnings in the first place.

What is "phantom income" and how can I owe tax if I broke even?

Once your losses are at least 90% of your winnings — meaning you broke even or lost money overall — your deduction is capped at exactly 90% of winnings no matter how much more you actually lost. The remaining 10% of winnings is taxed with no loss to offset it, and it does not carry forward. A gambler who wins $50,000 and loses $50,000 now owes tax on $5,000 of income despite walking away even.

Is this permanent, or does it expire like other OBBBA provisions?

It is permanent law with no scheduled sunset, unlike several other OBBBA individual-tax provisions (the SALT cap increase and the tips/overtime deductions both expire after 2028 or 2029). Multiple repeal bills, including one nicknamed the FAIR BET Act, have been introduced in Congress, but none had passed as of this tool's last fact-check — treat repeal as a watch item, not current law.

Do I need to itemize to claim any gambling-loss deduction?

Yes — this rule predates OBBBA and is unaffected by it. Gambling losses are only deductible on Schedule A, Line 16, for a taxpayer who itemizes. If you take the standard deduction, your full winnings are taxable and none of your losses offset them, cap or no cap.

Does this apply to professional gamblers too?

Yes. OBBBA permanently folded a professional gambler's trade-or-business wagering expenses into this same Section 165(d) limitation — a rule that was otherwise set to expire after 2025. A professional's wagering losses and directly related business expenses are grouped together and capped at 90% of winnings, the same as a casual gambler's losses alone.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal 90%-of-winnings cap to the numbers you enter. It does not verify your winnings, losses, itemizing decision, or filing status, and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

This calculator vs. working out the 90% gambling loss cap by hand

The rule sounds simple — "you can only deduct 90% of your losses" — and that plain-English version is exactly the part that goes wrong. The 90% applies to winnings, not losses, and getting that backwards changes the answer whenever the two numbers differ.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Which figure gets the 90%Takes 90% of losses, not winnings.Caps the deduction at the lesser of actual losses or 90% of WINNINGS — the two give different answers whenever losses and winnings differ.
The older rule underneathForgets losses were already capped at winnings before OBBBA, and applies only the new 90% rule.Applies both caps and reports whichever one actually binds — usually the new 90% figure once losses reach or exceed winnings.
Itemizing requirementAssumes some deduction is available either way.Reports zero deduction and full taxable winnings if you are not itemizing — a pre-OBBBA rule this new cap does not change.
Professional gamblersAssumes a trade-or-business structure escapes the cap.Flags that OBBBA permanently folds a professional's wagering-related business expenses into the same 90%-of-winnings limitation.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Applying the 90% to the wrong figure. The cap is 90% of WINNINGS, not 90% of losses — the deduction is the lesser of your actual losses or 90% of your winnings. Taking 90% of a large loss figure and comparing that to winnings gives the wrong answer whenever losses exceed winnings by more than a little.

What's the second most common mistake?

Forgetting the pre-existing rule is still there underneath the new one. Losses have always been capped at winnings, full stop — OBBBA adds a SECOND, tighter cap (90% of winnings) on top of that first one. Only the tighter of the two ever actually binds.

What eligibility mistake gets made most often?

Assuming any deduction is available without itemizing. It is not, and this predates OBBBA entirely — a non-itemizer's full winnings are taxable with zero loss offset, cap or no cap.

What mistake do professional gamblers make most often?

Assuming a trade-or-business structure escapes the cap. It does not — OBBBA permanently folded a professional gambler's wagering-related business expenses into the same 90%-of-winnings limitation a casual gambler's losses face.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your other itemized deductions, your state's own gambling-loss rules, or whether a repeal bill has since become law. Both apply the same published federal rule to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.
